In that world, it is much smarter to train the people you have today to become that “someone who knows how to use AI” and then pay them higher wages. You see, another metric that you are valued on is revenue per employee. If the revenue per employee doubles from your team becoming experts at AI leverage, you can pay that person a higher salary because they used AI to create the higher revenue per employee, while still driving your Rule of 40 way up. Replacing people entirely with AI for that profile of company is risky and slow. But bringing in experts to help that person become a power user of AI to accelerate your business is safe and fast. On the other hand, if you are a giant company with billions in revenue and a 5 percent growth rate and deep market penetration, meaning little market left to get, and for each market share you grab, you are often taking it from a giant competitor under tremendous downward pricing pressure. In that arena, which is a small percentage of companies by number, the smart move is to leverage AI to radically reduce your cost. And that leverage can be done in two ways: first, to be able to take market share from your giant competitors by reducing price faster than they can and perhaps driving your growth rate to twice its historical number; and second, by reducing cost more than you reduce price, which also drives up your profitability. In giant multibillion-dollar companies, small percentage movements represent very large dollars. And those companies always have enough people around to oversee the AI. If there is a department with 1,500 people, perhaps only 250 would be required to manage AI to take over the function. So, I strongly suggest that if you feel at risk, be aware of where on that continuum your company sits and think about what moves you can make now to position yourself to be on the winning side of this transition process. To some degree, that’s what this book is trying to help with. If you can develop a strong perspective on what AI is and how to begin to plug into it, you can thrive in this new world order. AI being able to do virtually all jobs is a different geopolitical discussion that we will take on in a bit. And today, plugging in is much more exciting and accessible than learning Lotus 1-2-3 before WYSIWYG. Younger readers might not get that acronym. But just plug it into a chat AI, and it will explain. As Jensen Huang, the CEO of NVIDIA, points out, there has never been a technology that is more easily accessible to use than AI chatbots—you just talk to it. 83 The Intern In early 2024, another of my sons completed an internship at my company. He was tasked with organizing all of our contracts. He used AI to teach him how to use another AI to quickly write a program (no coding skills required) to automate the task. It looked like magic, but it was just leverage. He had bypassed the energy constraints of manual sorting by plugging into AI. Many years earlier, the CFO of the real estate company thought a digital spreadsheet was magic. Forty years later, my son’s colleagues thought his AI automation was magic. The tool changes, but the feeling of friction disappearing remains the same. We are rapidly entering a time when the world rewards those who learn how to leverage AI. Rethinking Education Another of my college-aged sons got frustrated early in college because he was being forced to take general classes before getting into his major. So, he used AI to create a custom course for him to do on the side, with weekly projects and learning, so that he could get more exposure to his career faster. Our educational system needs to abandon the notion that using AI is cheating. Instead, we must embrace it as a tool for learning—a partner in cognitive development. We need to design tasks that teach students how to truly learn with AI. We need to acknowledge that the students now have a brilliant and patient thought partner at their side in all learning and nurture its use to expand curiosity and growth. And this shift doesn’t start in classrooms or institutions. It starts with each of us. To truly learn with AI, we must stop treating it like a search engine. Begin with curiosity, not commands. Frame your learning as a dialogue. Ask AI to explain a concept, then ask it to challenge your understanding. Try teaching it what you think you know—and let it find the gaps. And most importantly, take charge of your own learning. Don’t wait for a course or a curriculum or a work task to guide you. The era we’re entering rewards those who know how to ask better questions . The ones who lead and thrive aren’t those who know the most—but those who know how to learn very fast with their AI partner. Treat AI like a mirror, a mentor, and a sparring partner. Let it expand your understanding—not to replace your curiosity but to deeply engage it. Imagine being able to learn anything that you are curious about with an expert in that area to guide you, patiently and purposefully. This is a concept that our educational institutions simply must embrace to stay relevant.
